newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Electricidad de Caracas hopeful on new rate system.
newsitem.headline: Electricidad de Caracas hopeful on new rate system.

text.p: Leading Venezuelan utility and bellwether stock Electricidad de Caracas said it was concerned by Energy Minister Erwin Arrieta's Tuesday announcement there would be no immediate electricity rate rise, but is holding its fire for the time being.
"We would be more worried if nothing had happened by mid-February," said a company source, who declined to be identified.

A rate rise for January had been widely expected this week and Arrieta's denial came as a surprise. But besides the timing of a rate rise is a new system of setting tariffs that Electricidad hopes will eventually give it reasonable returns.
"... If the government applies the same seriousness to rate increases as it has recently to labor problems, we remain optimistic," one senior company official told Reuters.
The government's firm resolve in stonewalling union demands has boosted analysts' confidence in Venezuela's economic reforms.
But they add the same firmness has yet to be seen in Energy Minister Arrieta, whom leading financial magazine VenEconomy repeatedly labels "a cabinet non-reformer".
Under a new electricity regulatory framework, published in November, the old painstaking system for calculating electricity rate increases was scuttled.
Originally designed to automatically compensate utilities for inflation-based losses, the system was only ever belatedly applied.
That led last year to increasingly heated exchanges between a testy Electricidad and a recalcitrant Energy Ministry as inflation ratcheted up over 100 percent.

The company cut back its investment program as losses mounted. And it suspended dividend payments for most of the year, reinstating them only after receiving a 10.4 percent tariff increase in October.
The new regulations provide some light, and analysts have welcomed their general outline, which is designed to attract foreign investment to a crisis-ridden sector.

But they note a clear rate-setting system has yet to be written. Instead, the government has plugged the gap with an interim rule of thumb: rates that provide a nine percent return on electric company assets.
"The new tariff structure, based on return of assets, does not appear to be an integral part of the new framework," wrote InvestAnalysis consultant Alex Dalmady in a recent report.
"The (nine percent) formula seems to be a stop-gap measure," he added.
Despite the legal vacuum, Electricidad says it is comfortable, at least on a technical level, that government work on the new rate structure is proceeding apace.

"The authorities asked for, and got in November, all the information -- financial, efficiency and management -- they needed from electricity companies. That's good, a regulator needs such things," said the spokesperson.
But "rate setting is still a political, not a technical, decision at the Ministry's discretion, and that's what finally counts," she added.
Investors nevertheless remain sanguine. The stock, still the most liquid on the bolsa, is often used as a proxy by investors to buy into Venezuela's economic turnaround.

And Spanish investment house Santander, which recently increased its exposure to Venezuela through the $338 million purchase of leading local retail bank Banco de Venezuela, continues to rate EDC as overweight.
Falling inflation "should facilitate EDC passing on cost increases to customers," it said in a recent research report.
Inflation is expected to drop to around 25 percent in 1997.

Electricidad may also benefit from the government's current inflation-fighting, strong bolivar policy. Bolivar appreciation should "benefit the company, whose balance sheet contains more than $300 million in debt," said Santander.

"In addition, U.S. dollar investors will benefit from the flow of earnings in bolivars," the report said, adding, "EDC's estimated firm value/EBITDA for 1997 is 3.9 times, one half the regional average."
((-- Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2600))
